extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and readers learning practical criticism and close reading of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for critics and readers on how to approach, evaluate, and teach the reading of poetry, emphasizing pitfalls of simple rules and the need for careful, experience-informed judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge poetry solely by the value of its subject
rubrics_metrics.description: poetry is in the value of its subject. ... He picks out something he can call the subject. ... He can then argue 'It is good to lie and look at clouds; this poem conveys the experience of lying and looking at clouds; therefore, this poem is good.' ... Or conversely: 'Lying and looking at clouds is a commonplace and trivial activity; this poem represents such an activity; therefore, this poem is commonplace and trivial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid concluding a poem's merit only from the worth or interest of its subject-matter; faithful depiction of a 'bad' subject does not make the poem bad. Consider more than subject-identification when evaluating value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid evaluating poetry primarily by its 'message' or inspirational content
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader finds, or fails to find, something in the poem which seems to him 'an inspiring message,' and argues from the presence or absence of this 'inspirational bit' to the value or lack of value of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'quest for a message' or the preconception that poetry's value lies in its power to inspire blinds readers to other virtues; inspiration may occur but should not be the default test of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat particular qualities (e.g. 'lilt', 'vivid', 'musical', 'sincere') as independent universal tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Lilt is an excellent thing in its due place, but it does not give value to poetry unless the rest of the poem requires it, accords with it, conditions it and justifies it. ... So too will theories that poetry must be 'vivid,' 'simple,' 'musical,' 'stirring,' 'passionate,' 'sensuous,' 'impersonal,' or 'sincere' ... enable us to conclude quickly (and mistakenly) whether the poetry is good or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such qualities as context-dependent resources, not as stand-alone criteria; ask whether a quality is demanded and justified by the poem's whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of applying simple 'key-words' or critical maxims uncritically
rubrics_metrics.description: Most critical key-words excel in this duplicity, as we have seen with 'sentimental' and with 'sincere.' Supplied with one of these words — 'sincere' is a great favourite — we have the poem up before us and apply the test. There will probably be from seven to eleven senses ... all confusedly among the possibilities of the word in the context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the multiple senses and ambiguities of critical terms; avoid assuming a single unambiguous meaning and using such words as mechanical tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer complex, qualified accounts over simple direct 'keys'
rubrics_metrics.description: But if what we are seeking is not a key, but an understanding of the whole matter, and particularly of the reasons why no such keys can be used, then the trouble is very well rewarded. ... Alternatives, conditions, qualifications, compensating conditions ... force themselves into it under the pressure of the facts, until it becomes evident that a direct practical application of an adequate account to any poem is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value analytic complexity and nuanced distinctions; accept that useful accounts will be intricate and resist naive direct application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value often turns on minute particulars and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Value in poetry turns nearly always upon differences and connections too minute and unobtrusive to be directly perceived. We recognise them only in their effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend closely to subtle details and their cumulative effects; hold the whole poem in mind as a living experience rather than relying on coarse features alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical judgment ultimately involves a direct personal choice
rubrics_metrics.description: There comes a point in all criticism where a sheer choice has to be made without the support of any arguments, principles, or general rules. All that arguments or principles can do is to protect us from irrelevancies ... They certainly can prevent us from judging by the detail rather than by the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that after careful attention and analysis a genuine act of selection by the critic's personality is necessary and unavoidable; do not expect rules to determine the final verdict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use arguments and principles to guard against irrelevancies, not to replace choice
rubrics_metrics.description: All that arguments or principles can do is to protect us from irrelevancies, red-herrings and disturbing preconceptions. They may remind us perhaps, that every poem has many more aspects than are presented on one occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ analysis and principles as tools to expand awareness and avoid mistakes, but do not let them substitute for the critic's engaged decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid converting choice into mechanical judgment by doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: All critical doctrines are attempts to convert choice into what may seem a safer activity — the reading evidence and the application of rules and principles. They are an invasion into an inappropriate sphere ... The result of doctrine is to transform what was choice into judgment. Judgment in these matters is not a refinement upon choice ... but a degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of doctrines that promise safety; doctrines may disguise vagueness and reduce the living act of choice to formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop the craft of 'construing' meaning — it is teachable and necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: This construing ... is not nearly so easy and 'natural' a performance as we tend to assume. It is a craft, in the sense that mathematics, cooking, and shoemaking are crafts. It can be taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include systematic instruction and practice in techniques for construing (interpreting) poems as part of literary education; do not assume meaning-construction happens automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate general maturity and life experience to inform judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: First may be placed the general immaturity of the readers. ... one important reason for erratic opinions seems undeniably to be lack of general experience. ... The years will do their work, for good and ill, but in others there is little reason to expect any essential change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that emotional and life experience influence the ability to judge poetry; encourage broader experience and development as part of training readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build wide reading background to avoid naive identifications and false impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: A lack of experience with poetry must be placed next to general inexperience of life in this list of deficiencies. ... those readers who did try to use their background often proved the naivety of their outlook and the poverty of their literary experience by the comparisons and identifications they made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage extensive and varied reading so readers can recognise originality, echoes, and influences rather than being misled by superficial resemblances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combat stock responses and inappropriate acquired reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Closely connected with this incapacity to apprehend unusual meanings is the fatal facility with which usual meanings reappear when they are not wanted. Great stress was laid ... upon this tendency of our acquired responses to intervene in situations to which they are not appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train readers to notice when habitual responses are being inappropriately applied and to hold back stock reactions in order to apprehend unique or unfamiliar meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of preconceptions, tests, and critical maxims that hide what is present
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain tests, criteria and presuppositions as to what is to be admired or despised in poetry proved their power to hide what was actually present. ... Without some objective criteria ... he feels like a friendless man deprived of weapons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the double-edged nature of criteria: they may help the inexperienced feel equipped, but they often occlude the poem; aim to rely on one's available experience rather than rigid maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise authority bias — poet's reputation colors response
rubrics_metrics.description: Far more than we like to admit, we take a hint for our response from the poet's reputation. Whether we assent or dissent, the traditional view runs through our response like the wire upon which a climbing plant is trained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to read at least sometimes without knowledge of authorship or reputation to test how much authority shapes approval; be cautious about letting reputation substitute for attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for variability and contingencies of critical capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: It was interesting to observe the wide range of quality that many individual readers varied through. ... Some of these unevennesses may be put down to fatigue. ... 'Making up our minds about a poem' is the most delicate of all possible undertakings. ... Health, wakefulness, distractions, hunger and other instinctive tensions ... all affect us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that a reader's response may vary with time, condition, context and environment; avoid overinterpreting a single response as definitive and be prudent about reading conditions (e.g., avoid fatigue).

rubrics_metrics.name: When readers are bewildered, provide instructive preparation rather than simplistic maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: But this advice, however well meant, can perhaps only further perplex that great body of readers whose first and last reaction to poetry ... is bewilderment. ... It should surely be possible ... to prepare them better, and make them more reasonably self-reliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design teaching/technique that prepares readers to face difficult poems (contextual clues, interpretive techniques) rather than leaving them dependent on authority or empty maxims.
